outcomes.text: Listen carefully to unfamiliar music from all four areas of study and describe its elements, context and language.
Use staff notation when describing unfamiliar music from any area of study.
Appraise the set study pieces for two areas of study, one being Area of study 1.
Explain how audience, time and place shaped how the study pieces were created, developed and performed.
Explain how and why the music has changed over time and how composer intention shows in musical elements.

topics.title: 3.1.2 Area of study 1: Western classical tradition 1650-1910

subtopics.title: Styles of the western classical tradition

outcomes.text: Describe music of Handel's anthems and oratorios, orchestral music of Haydn, Mozart and Beethoven, piano music of Chopin and Schumann, and the late Romantic Requiem.
Appraise the set study pieces by Mozart and Beethoven in their context.

subtopics.title: Melody and harmony in classical music

outcomes.text: Describe melody types such as conjunct, disjunct, scalic and arpeggio, plus passing notes, ornaments and ostinato.
Describe harmony: diatonic and chromatic, consonant and dissonant, pedal and drone, and the main cadences.
Identify major, minor and dominant seventh chords by chord symbols or roman numerals.
Describe major and minor keys up to four sharps and flats, modulation to related keys, and relative keys.
Recognise structures such as binary, ternary, rondo, sonata, theme and variations, ground bass and cadenza.
Describe textures such as homophonic, polyphonic, imitative, canonic, antiphonal and melody with accompaniment.
Describe instruments, voices and techniques such as arco, pizzicato and con sordino in solo, concerto and chamber music.
Describe simple and compound time, anacrusis, hemiola, dotted rhythms, triplets, rubato and Italian tempo terms.
Read and use dynamics and articulation markings from pp to ff, crescendo, diminuendo and sforzando.
Identify musical elements when reading unfamiliar staff notation of up to 12 bars.
Write melodies up to four sharps or flats and rhythms in simple and compound time in staff notation of up to eight bars.
Learn major and minor chords and identify them by ear and in notation.
Use appropriate musical vocabulary for music heard and notated.
Describe Broadway music of the 1950s to 1990s, 1960s-70s rock, film and gaming music, and pop since the 1990s.
Appraise the set popular music study pieces in their context.
Describe melody devices such as riff, hook, pitch bend, melisma, glissando, improvisation and blue notes.
Describe power chords, chord symbols, stock progressions, pentatonic, modal and blues scales.
Describe song structures such as verse, chorus, break, intro, outro, twelve-bar blues and drum fill.
Describe contemporary instruments, vocal timbres, guitar and drum techniques, amplification, distortion and recording effects.
Describe tempo and rhythm terms such as bpm, groove, backbeat, syncopation, off-beat and swing.
Describe blues from 1920-1950, African and Caribbean fusion, contemporary Latin and British Isles folk music.
Appraise the set traditional music study pieces in their context.
Describe melody and tonality: blue notes, pentatonic, whole tone, modal, scat, melisma and improvisation.
Describe structures such as strophic, cyclic, call and response, popular song forms and 12 or 16 bar blues.
Describe world instrument families, technology and effects, drone, vocal techniques and textures such as layering.
Describe rhythms such as clave, polyrhythm, cross-rhythm, syncopation, bossa nova, samba, salsa, tango and rumba.

topics.title: 3.1.6 Area of study 4: Western classical tradition since 1910

outcomes.text: Describe orchestral music of Copland, British music of Arnold, Britten, Maxwell-Davies and Tavener, Kodaly and Bartok, and minimalism.
Appraise the set study pieces by Kodaly and Bartok in their context.
Describe melody and harmony devices such as ostinato, motifs, melisma, chromatic, dissonant and pedal.
Describe tonality including pentatonic, whole tone, modal and tonal ambiguity.
Describe sonority, technology, drones, imitative and layered textures.
Describe irregular, free, polyrhythmic and syncopated rhythm, hemiola, rubato and anacrusis.
Identify musical elements when reading unfamiliar staff notation of up to 12 bars.
Learn major and minor chords and their symbols and identify them by ear and in notation.
Use appropriate musical vocabulary for music heard and notated in the chosen area of study.
Perform live as a soloist and in an ensemble, as instrumental, vocal or DJ performers or through music production.
Interpret musical elements with accurate technical control, expression, phrasing and dynamics suited to the style.
Support recorded performances with a score, lead sheet, guide recording or annotation.
Perform a solo with secure pitch, rhythm, fluency, tempo, dynamics and articulation.
Perform in an ensemble where each performer has a unique and significant role.
Perform as a solo or ensemble DJ using turntables or digital DJ technology with at least two beat-matched tracks.
Use basic DJ skills: cue stuttering, spin-backs, drop-ins and EQ blending or effects.
Use intermediate skills: baby scratches, looping, hot cues and a cappella sources.
Use advanced skills: transforms, flares, chirps, orbits, hot-cue drumming and juggling.
Work with sound sources such as tracks, scratch samples, loops and a cappellas.
Perform a solo piece using technology, sequencing or multi-tracking with at least three tracks, one live.
Perform an ensemble piece through production with at least four tracks, including live tracks from the student and others.
Develop, extend and manipulate musical ideas to compose music that is convincing.
Write one composition to an externally set brief and one free composition, of any style.
Use at least four musical elements per composition, with two from rhythm, metre, texture, melody, structure or form and two from harmony, tonality, timbre, dynamics, phrasing or articulation.
Compose using methods suited to the style, such as notation software, sequencing, multi-tracking or improvisation.
Write a programme note of about 150 words giving intention, audience, chosen elements and software and hardware used.
Support each composition with a score, lead sheet or aural guide.
